# Slugs and snails in beds

Slugs and snails feed at night and hide by day in cool damp places — under pots, dense mulch and boards. Ragged holes in young leaves and seedlings sheared off overnight, with a silvery mucus trail in the morning, identify them before the pests are ever seen. Tender crops like lettuce, hostas and brassica seedlings suffer most; established plants usually survive grazing.

Control works best layered. Beer traps — shallow dishes sunk to soil level and filled with beer — lure them in and they drown, though the range is short so place several among the vulnerable plants. Iron phosphate granules are the effective bait labeled for food beds; scatter them thinly around plants after rain and repeat after watering, since they degrade. Copper barrier tape around pots and raised bed rims gives a mild electric repulsion on contact, and collars of cut bottles protect individual seedlings until they toughen.

Habitat work reduces the population more than trapping alone. Remove boards and debris piles where they shelter, water in the morning so the surface is dry at night, and keep dense mulch a hand's width from stems of susceptible crops. Ducks patrol beds enthusiastically, and ground beetles and frogs are free predators worth encouraging. Handpicking by flashlight an hour after dark still outperforms most other methods on a small plot.
